text: Every demo I've taken apart on this channel was made in Unity, by people who write code. This one wasn't.
It was made in a tool sold on the promise that you never have to program. There's a C# compiler inside the build anyway.
Veiled Shadows is a month in a rural mountain town. You build bonds during the day, and at night you go into another world.
Everyone who has played it reaches for the same word: Persona. One reviewer counted the nods to Persona 4.
The battle menu is drawn as a handheld console, and your abilities are cartridges you slot into it.
The demo went up five days ago. Six reviews, all positive. That's not a reception, so what I can actually read here is the build.
Steam publishes the file list for every demo. This one has seventy one entries.
The engine is RPG Developer Bakin, from a Japanese studio called SmileBoom. Seventy dollars on Steam, and it's sold as programming-free RPG creation.
The game's own executable is five hundred and sixty two kilobytes. It's a launcher.
What actually runs the game is bakinplayer.exe, and the engine DLL sitting next to it.
Then there's one file that is the entire game.
data.rbpack. One point three five gigabytes. Ninety five percent of the download.
Every map, every model, every portrait and every voice line this person made is inside that one file.
The other seventy entries are the engine, shipped exactly as it arrived.
Which is the interesting part, because of what a no-code tool puts in your game without asking.
First. Microsoft.CodeAnalysis, two DLLs, ten point seven megabytes. That's Roslyn. That is a C# compiler.
Bakin does offer an optional C# scripting feature, and this is what pays for it. Every game made in the tool carries a compiler, whether its author wrote a line of C# or not.
Second. WebView2, and an Edge browser control. There is a web browser inside this turn-based RPG.
I could not work out what it's for from a file list. If you've built something in Bakin, the comments are right there.
Third, and this is the one worth taking away. VRM Loader.
VRM is the avatar format VRoid Studio exports. The format VTubers use.
So a solo developer can pull a 3D character out of an avatar maker instead of modelling one from scratch.
The shaders ship as plain text, uncompiled. Seven include files, thirty eight kilobytes between them. One is six bytes long.
They get compiled on your machine when you play. That's what the seventeen megabyte DirectX shader compiler next to them is for.
And there's a log file in there. bakinplayer_log.txt, from the developer's own session, shipped to players.
It's fourteen kilobytes. Two episodes ago the same mistake was seven hundred and seventy megabytes of debug symbols. Four orders of magnitude apart.

There are four readme files too, in English, Japanese and both kinds of Chinese, on a store page that lists English only. Those are the engine's own readmes, which tells you the folder went out untouched.
Now the six reviews. You can't count six of anything, but you can read them.
One of them tells me the developer is one person in Austria. That's the team size, from a player, not a press kit.
Two of them mention the voice acting, unprompted. And one had seven hours on a demo that covers a few in-game days.
Here's the whole teardown on one card.
Bakin, seventy dollars, one person. One point three five gigabytes of their content against sixty seven megabytes of engine they didn't write.
Worth a dip, and worth it for the art alone.
If somebody has told you no-code means a low ceiling, this build ships a C# compiler. The ceiling is wherever you stop.

And before you publish, open your engine folder. That's my read from the outside, though. If you made this and I got something wrong, say so and I'll pin the correction. Next time, another demo, another file list. This is Demo Dip.
